questions.stem: A 37-year-old woman presented with a rash on her finger. It had been present for 2 months and had not improved. There was no history of fevers, and the rash was not painful or draining. She had a past medical history of type 2 diabetes. She lived in Chicago and had not travelled in recent years. She was a carpenter and recalled pulling a wooden splinter out of that finger about 1 month before the rash developed. She lived with her partner and 8-year-old son, who were both well. They had a pet dog and cat that were healthy and owned several exotic fish; the patient sometimes helped her son clean the tank. On examination, there was an erythematous lesion that was not tender, warm, or fluctuant. There were no other skin lesions present. Investigations: Plain radiograph of the hand showed no fracture or foreign body.
questions.lead_in: What is the most appropriate treatment?
questions.explanation: Itraconazole The most likely diagnosis in this case is sporotrichosis, notably the fixed cutaneous form as there is no mention of the typical lymphangitic pattern of nodules along the ipsilateral limb. Although she does occasionally clean her son’s fish tank (consider Mycobacterium marinum ) and owns a cat (consider Bartonella henselae or cat scratch disease) the most important clue is the history of the wooden splinter that she removed from her finger one month prior to this, suggesting direct inoculation with Sporothrix. It is also possible, and often more common, for cats to transmit Sporothrix with a scratch (particularly cats that spend time outdoors with soil contamination of their claws); although still plausible, there is no mention of a cat scratch. The prolonged duration of symptoms and findings argue against this being a pyogenic (e.g., staphylococcal) infection. Sporotrichosis does not resolve without treatment. A skin biopsy for histopathology and fungal culture should confirm the diagnosis. Treatment with itraconazole is recommended for a total duration of 3–6 months until all lesions have fully resolved for at least 2–4 weeks. (Image from Cohen BA. Nodules and tumors. In Pediatric Dermatology. 4th ed. Elsevier; 2013.)
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 4 Q30

questions.question: [image-based question: Picture of man with nodular lymphangitis. Has aquarium.]

parts.text: Give a differential of four possible causes of this clinical picture.
Given that he has an aquarium, which is most likely?
How would you diagnose this?

cohort_answer.text: Differential: Mycobacterium marinum; Sporothrix schenckii; Nocardia brasiliensis; Leishmania braziliensis; Tularemia; Systemic mycoses. Most likely: Mycobacterium marinum. Diagnosis: Biopsy for AFB and culture + histopath. Treatment: surgical debridement/excision should suffice, if invasive, give rifampin + ethambutol +/- macrolide

questions.question: 18.  Picture of nodular lymphangitis, give four organisms.

parts.text: [image-based question: photo of nodular lymphangitis] Give four organisms.

cohort_answer.text: Mycobacterium marinum; Nocardia brasiliensis; Leishmania braziliensis; Sporothrix schenkii

parts.text: What treatment would you start if the gram stain showed long gram positive bacilli?
What treatment would you start if the gram stain showed yeast?

cohort_answer.text: Long GPB: TMP-SMX/imipenem/amikacin for ?nocardia; ?anthrax for cipro/doxy. || Yeast: Sporothrix schenkii, itraconazole.

questions.question: [image-based question: photo of a person with nodular lymphangitis on arm]

parts.text: Name 4 potential pathogens.

cohort_answer.text: Nocardia, Mycobacterium marinum, Leishmania, Sporothrix (also Tularemia, Leprosy, Bartonella)

questions.question: PM 1. Lady who develops lesions after cleaning fish tank. Picture of sporotrichoid rash. [image-based question: sporotrichoid rash]

parts.text: What is the organism? (1)
What are TWO options for monotherapy? (2)
What are 3 other organisms that give lymphocutaneous spread? (1.5)

cohort_answer.text: Mycobacterium marinum. Monotherapy options: Clarithromycin, or Doxycycline/Minocycline, or Septra for minimum 3 months; rifampin plus ethambutol. Other lymphocutaneous organisms: Francisella tularensis, Nocardia brasiliensis, Mycobacterium marinum, other NTM, Sporothrix schenckii, Leishmaniasis, Bacillus anthracis. (Note: Sandford combination therapy is 2 active agents for 1-2 months after resolution of skin lesion: Clarithromycin 500mg BID + ethambutol 25mg/kg/day, or Rifampin 600mg q24h + ethambutol 25mg/kg/day; Hopkins offers monotherapy alternatives: minocycline 100 BID, doxycycline 100 BID, Septra DS BID.)

questions.question: Renal transplant, diabetic, and cut hand at lake house. 1 Week later got papules and ulcerative lesions on the hand and arm. There is no lymph involvement. Pathology shows granulomatous inflammation with soccer ball appearance (morulae). AFB and bacterial negative. Sabouraud agar shows white fluffy colony at 6 days.

parts.text: What is the most likely genus?
What group of organisms does this belong to?
What are two treatment?

questions.model_answer:
a) Most likely genus: Prototheca (most human infections due to P. wickerhamii).
b) Group of organisms: achlorophyllous (non-photosynthetic) algae - Prototheca is a genus of algae (related to Chlorella) that has lost chlorophyll and can act as an opportunistic human pathogen, particularly after cutaneous inoculation in immunocompromised hosts (e.g., water/trauma exposure in a renal transplant/diabetic patient). Its characteristic tissue morphology is the sporangium containing internally septated endospores in a symmetric "morula"/soccer-ball pattern.
c) Two treatment options: surgical excision/debridement of the lesion, combined with systemic antifungal therapy such as amphotericin B (or itraconazole/posaconazole).
questions.beyond_mandell: This vignette (protothecosis) is a mismatch with the assigned Sporothrix schenckii chapter; answered from general mycology/algology knowledge rather than this Mandell chapter.

questions.question: [image-based question: 33 yo guy cleaning fish tanks. Picture of hand with Sporotrichoid spread.]

parts.text: 4 organisms which can cause this type of presentation.

questions.model_answer: Four organisms causing a sporotrichoid (nodular lymphangitic) spread pattern: Sporothrix schenckii, Mycobacterium marinum (classically associated with fish tank/aquarium exposure), Nocardia brasiliensis, and Leishmania braziliensis (cutaneous/sporotrichoid leishmaniasis).

questions.question: Picture of nodular lymphangitis of the arm. They take a sample for microbiologic testing. They give you four images of stains and you have to identify the organism in each stain that would cause these lesions (something like these pictures)

parts.text: [image-based question: Gram stain - gram positive cocci (could not agree whether clusters or chains)]
[image-based question: Gram Stain - Branching gram positive bacilli]
[image-based question: H&E stain]
[image-based question: Grocott Gomori Methenamine Silver Stain - Yeast]

questions.model_answer:
a) Gram stain showing gram-positive cocci (in clusters or chains): suggests a bacterial cause of nodular lymphangitis such as Staphylococcus aureus (clusters) or Streptococcus pyogenes (chains).
b) Gram stain showing branching, beaded gram-positive bacilli: Nocardia brasiliensis (also weakly acid-fast/modified acid-fast positive).
c) H&E stain: cigar-shaped budding yeast forms consistent with Sporothrix schenckii (though organisms are often sparse and difficult to visualize on H&E).
d) GMS (Grocott-Gomori methenamine silver) stain showing yeast: Sporothrix schenckii (cigar-shaped budding yeast highlighted well by GMS when H&E is unrevealing).
questions.beyond_mandell: Without the actual images, the gram stain organism identifications (a, b) are inferred from the classic sporotrichoid/nodular lymphangitis differential rather than directly confirmed.

questions.question: [image-based question: picture of sporotrichoid spread with 4 different stains shown, asked to identify the organism for each]

parts.text: Stain 1 (Leischmania)
Stain of nocardia branching GPCs in chains
A gram stain with 30% GPC, rest looked either washed out or like GNC either solo or in short chains, clusters as well (Francisella tularensis)
Sporothrix stain, ~2microns in size (given legend up to 20 microns, nothing over 2-3 microns in size)

cohort_answer.text: Stain 1: Leishmania. Stain 2: Nocardia (branching GPCs in chains). Stain 3: Francisella tularensis (gram stain with ~30% GPC, rest washed out/GNC solo or in short chains/clusters). Stain 4: Sporothrix (~2 microns in size).

questions.question: Q92 2023 Day 2. [image-based question: photomicrographs/stains shown with a sporotrichoid spread pattern; 4 different images shown and the candidate is asked to identify the organism for each]

parts.text: Identify the organism shown in image 1 (H&E stain)
Identify the organism shown in image 2 (branching gram-positive rods)
Identify the organism shown in image 3 (tiny gram-negative coccobacilli, no growth on MacConkey)
Identify the organism shown in image 4 (PAS stain with budding yeast-like cells and conidiophores)

cohort_answer.text:
Image 1: Leishmania spp. amastigotes, H&E stain - spherical to ovoid, 1-5 µm long by 1-2 µm wide, large nucleus, prominent kinetoplast, short axoneme (rarely visible by light microscopy); reside in macrophages.
Image 2: Nocardia - branching, filamentous, beaded, gram-positive rods with right angle branching (compare/contrast with Rhodococcus equi).
Image 3: Francisella tularensis - tiny, gram-negative coccobacilli, no growth on MacConkey; 'junky' gram stain of tiny GNCB's, DDx Francisella or Brucella; oxidase negative, urease negative, weakly catalase positive, strict aerobes.
Image 4: Sporothrix schenckii - small (~2 microns); PAS stained tissue section showing budding yeast-like cells; conidiophores and conidia are ovoid, elongated, 3-6 x 2-3 µm, one-celled, smooth walled, hyaline.
